content: Pneumonia caused by bacterial pathogens is the leading cause of death in children in low-income countries. Early administration of antibiotics significantly improves clinical outcomes in these cases. The objective of this study was to identify the most effective antibiotic therapies for community-acquired pneumonia (CAP) of varying severity in children by comparing different antibiotics. The researchers conducted a comprehensive search of multiple databases, including CENTRAL, MEDLINE, EMBASE, CINAHL, Web of Science, and LILACS, covering studies published up to November 2012. They included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that compared at least two antibiotics for the treatment of CAP in children, either in hospital or outpatient settings. A total of 29 trials involving 14,188 children were included in the analysis. None of the studies compared antibiotics with placebo. The quality of the studies was assessed, and five of the 29 studies were double-blind with adequate allocation concealment. Another 12 studies were unblinded but had adequate allocation concealment, classifying them as good-quality studies. Comparisons between co-trimoxazole and amoxicillin, oral amoxicillin and injectable penicillin/ampicillin, and chloramphenicol and ampicillin/penicillin were supported by high-quality evidence. In outpatient settings, for the treatment of non-severe CAP as defined by the World Health Organization (WHO), amoxicillin and co-trimoxazole showed similar failure rates (odds ratio [OR] 1.18, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.91 to 1.51) and cure rates (OR 1.03, 95% CI 0.56 to 1.89). This conclusion was based on three studies involving 3,952 children. For children with severe pneumonia without hypoxemia, oral antibiotics such as amoxicillin or co-trimoxazole were found to have similar failure rates (OR 0.84, 95% CI 0.56 to 1.24), hospitalisation rates (OR 1.13, 95% CI 0.38 to 3.34), and relapse rates (OR 1.28, 95% CI 0.34 to 4.82) compared to injectable penicillin. This conclusion was based on six studies involving 4,331 children under 18 years of age. In cases of very severe CAP, children receiving chloramphenicol had higher death rates compared to those treated with a combination of penicillin/ampicillin and gentamicin (OR 1.25, 95% CI 0.76 to 2.07). This finding was based on one study involving 1,116 children. The authors concluded that for the treatment of CAP in outpatient settings, amoxicillin is a viable alternative to co-trimoxazole. In cases where data on other antibiotics are limited, co-amoxiclavulanic acid and cefpodoxime may serve as second-line options. Children with severe pneumonia without hypoxemia can be effectively treated with oral amoxicillin in outpatient settings. For hospitalised children with severe or very severe CAP, the combination of penicillin/ampicillin and gentamicin is superior to chloramphenicol. Co-amoxiclavulanic acid and cefuroxime may be considered as alternative second-line therapies for these patients. The authors emphasized the need for further studies involving larger patient populations with radiographically confirmed pneumonia and standardized methodologies to evaluate newer antibiotics. The recommendations in this review are particularly relevant for countries with high pneumonia-related mortality rates in children without underlying health conditions and where point-of-care diagnostic tests for identifying the causative agents of pneumonia are unavailable.
